Centralize cross-view data rules once.

Filtering, sorting, labels, and derived display values often begin as small template decisions and gradually diverge across screens. This chapter moves those rules into the pipeline, where a candidate collection can be refined once and its display-ready State can be reused by every consumer.

Why this boundary matters

Filters shape the candidate before reducers derive the committed value; neither stage belongs in a component template. Pure, service-registered functions keep the transformation order explicit, prevent repeated view logic, and let each consumer render the same refined and derived State.

Use this structure for

  • removing ineligible or incomplete records before they are rendered
  • sorting collections consistently across multiple views
  • deriving labels and display fields once for every consumer

By the end of this chapter

You will have a pure filter that refines candidate characters and ordered reducers that derive sorting, labels, and full names before the committed State reaches the component.

Step 20: Add the Filter Stage
↑ top

This chapter focuses on pipeline shaping. The service still owns the same , but now the incoming candidate collection is refined after the Resolve stage and before any reducer derives the final committed value.

That execution order matters. The filter stage runs after Resolve and before Reducers, so the candidate collection is refined before any reducer logic runs. In this example, the pure removeUnknownLastNameFilter removes any candidate character whose last name is exactly unknown, so the collection is cleaned before reducer logic derives any display fields.

Take Action
  1. Open example.filter.ts and add the pure filter that removes characters whose last name is unknown.
  2. Open example.service.ts and register that filter with this.#vault.filters().
What to Look For
  • The filter runs on the candidate collection produced after Resolve, not on the currently rendered template state.
  • The filter is pure and side-effect free: it returns a refined array and does not mutate the incoming candidate.
  • The service still owns pipeline registration. The component does not decide which characters are filtered.
  • Filter registration order is deterministic, so the reducer stage only sees the already-filtered candidate collection.
  • In the star-wars-character.constant.ts file there are 5 characters with Chewbacca's last name being unknown. The filter remove him from the candidate state request.

Step 21: Add Reducer Styles
↑ top

After the filter stage refines the candidate collection, reducers derive the display-ready state that the component will actually render. Here, you apply three reducer styles to the same post-filter candidate while keeping the same service-owned boundary.

The order is intentional and matches the pipeline documentation: reducers run after filters. The first reducer delegates to a pure helper that derives forceSensitiveDisplay. The second uses a factory function, withCharactersSortedByLastName(), to return a configured reducer. The third delegates again to deriveFullName so the committed snapshot carries a display-ready full name without pushing string composition into the template.

Take Action
  1. Open example.character-domain.ts and use the existing filter and reducer helpers for force-sensitive labels, last-name sorting, and full-name derivation.
  2. Register those reducers in example.service.ts in the exact order they should run.
Reducer Styles in This Chapter
  • Reducer 1 is a direct pure reducer helper: deriveForceSensitiveDisplay maps every character to a display-ready Yes or No label.
  • Reducer 2 is a factory-generated reducer: withCharactersSortedByLastName() returns a ReducerFunction that clones and sorts the collection immutably.
  • Reducer 3 is another direct pure reducer helper: deriveFullName derives the final display label that every view reuses.
  • Because reducers run after filters, each reducer works on the already refined candidate collection instead of repeating filter logic.

Step 22: Complete Filters and Reducers Chapter
↑ top

The filters and reducers chapter is complete once the page no longer composes display values in the template, the reducer-derived character fields drive the visible UI, and the filter and reducer source appears in text areas for direct comparison.

That is the key architectural result of this chapter. The component still owns selection, editor, and feedback state, but it now renders a collection that has already moved through Resolve, Filter, and Reducer stages. The template reads fullName and forceSensitiveDisplay directly instead of concatenating names or translating booleans inline, which keeps display rules inside the pipeline rather than scattered across markup.

  3. Verify that the displayed source views and reducer-driven UI values match the committed state.

  • The page now includes dedicated text areas that surface the filter and each reducer source for direct comparison.
  • The service now demonstrates pipeline-stage registration, not just CRUD mutations, while preserving the same service-owned boundary.
